gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Fluance RT81's built-in preamp is the same Texas Instruments stage with the same 140 mV (−17 dBV) line output as the RT81+. Secrets of Home Theater and High Fidelity's John E. Johnson, Jr. asked for 0.5 V from that preamp, which is about 11 dB more than it gives.
standout_why: I compared stylusandsound.com, platterandplinth.com and valveandvinyl.com, and tried fewbetter.com. Stylusandsound already gives the RT81+ line output as 140 mV and says to switch to LINE for the built-in preamp and PHONO to bypass it. Platterandplinth already explains the mechanism: LINE means the internal preamp does the RIAA correction and gain, and LINE into a PHONO input means 'amplified and RIAA-corrected twice'. Valveandvinyl gives Audio-Technica's 36 dB gain and the RT81's true bypass. fewbetter.com is a homepage with no turntable content. None of them gives the plain RT81's line output in mV, names the Texas Instruments stage, or quotes a named reviewer saying the output is too low. So my angle adds only part of a fact that rivals mostly have already.
decides: It confirms the plan works. Every candidate can feed powered speakers or an AUX input once its switch is set to LINE. Both Fluance decks have the same preamp and the same 140 mV output, so the extra $50 for the RT81+ ($349.99 against $299.99 at fluance.com) buys cartridge and platter changes, not a stronger preamp. With low-sensitivity powered speakers, the shopper should expect to turn the volume up further with the Fluance decks. I could not confirm from a page I opened that the Audio-Technica AT-LP70X has more output, so I can't call it a deciding difference.

findings.note: By John E. Johnson, Jr., published 2016-06-15. My arithmetic: 20·log10(0.14 V / 0.5 V) = −11.1 dB, so Fluance's 140 mV is about 11 dB below the level the reviewer wanted. The review's own spec table labels the 140 mV as 'PHONO OUTPUT', but the maker's page lists it as the line output.
